title: Joining Letters
keyIdea: Where a letter finishes decides how it joins. Letters that end on the line with a flick, like a, i and n, make a diagonal join: a slanting stroke up to where the next letter starts. o, r, v and w end at the top, so they make a horizontal join across the top. The join climbs to the top of a small letter, or right up to the top of a tall letter's ascender. Break letters such as b, g, j, p, q, x, y and z are not joined from, though we still join to them. Keep small letters, ascenders and descenders the right size so joined writing stays easy to read.

kid: Joined writing is quicker because your pen does not keep lifting off. To join well, look at where each letter finishes. Some letters end on the line with a little flick up, like a, i, n and u. From these, the join slants up to the next letter. This is a diagonal join, as in in, un and al.

The letters o, r, v and w end at the top. From these, the join runs across the top, like a bridge. This is a horizontal join, as in on, ri and wh. Do not dip down to the line first. How high does the join go? To the top of a small letter like n. For a tall letter like l or h, it climbs right up to the top of the tall part, the ascender.
Some letters are break letters: b, g, j, p, q, x, y and z. We do not join from them. Leave a small gap after them. We can still join to them, so in gap the a joins to the p.
Keep sizes even. Small letters sit between the line and the dashed line. Tall letters reach the top line. Tails, called descenders, go below the line.
adult: The National Curriculum for England asks Year 2 pupils to start using some of the diagonal and horizontal strokes needed to join letters. They also learn which letters are best left unjoined when they sit next to each other. In Years 3 and 4, pupils use these joins in all their writing and keep ascenders and descenders in proportion. Schemes such as Nelson Handwriting teach four joins: diagonal to a small letter, diagonal to an ascender, horizontal to a small letter and horizontal to an ascender.

The rule underneath is the exit stroke. Letters that end on the baseline with a flick up, such as a, d, e, i, l, n and u, make diagonal joins. The letters o, r, v and w end at the x-height and make horizontal joins. The next letter sets the height: x-height for small letters, the top of the ascender for b, d, f, h, k, l and t. In Nelson style, b, g, j, p, q, x, y and z are break letters that we do not join from, and z is not joined to either. A few letters vary between schools, so follow your own school's style.

Common mistakes: dipping to the baseline after o or w, which turns a horizontal join into a loop; running the join flat along the line; stopping the join short of the ascender, so h looks like n; joining out of a break letter's tail; and letting small letters grow as tall as ascenders once joins are added. A common adult slip is to push joining before each letter is formed from the right starting point. That fixes poor letter shapes into the joins.

In the lab your child finds where four letters finish and drags diagonal and horizontal joins to the right height. Then they mark which gaps in jump, gap and boy join and which stay open, and spot letters drawn at the wrong size on the four handwriting lines.

familyTip: Write a short word together, like 'sun' or 'on', and ask "Where does this letter finish: on the line or at the top?" before joining. In shop lists and cards, praise even letter sizes as much as neat joins.

visual.caption: Which join? Drag each letter pair, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: drag diagonal and horizontal joins, gap the break letters, fix letter sizes.

practice.prompt: Which join do you use from o to n?
choices: A horizontal join across the top
A diagonal join up from the line
practice.hint: Where does o finish: on the line or at the top?
practice.explain: o finishes at the top, so the join runs across the top to n. That is a horizontal join.

practice.prompt: A word has {n} letters and no break letters. Every letter joins to the next. How many joins are there?
practice.hint: Count the gaps between letters, not the letters.
practice.explain: {n} letters have {=n-1} gaps between them, and each gap gets a join, so there are {=n-1} joins.

practice.prompt: In the word jump, which gap stays open?
practice.hint: Which of these letters is a break letter?
practice.explain: j is a break letter, so we do not join from it. u joins to m, and m joins to p, because we can join to a break letter.

practice.prompt: A word has {n} letters. Only the first letter is a break letter, and all the others join. How many joins are there?
practice.hint: Count the gaps, then take away the one after the break letter.
practice.explain: {n} letters have {=n-1} gaps. The gap after the break letter stays open, so there are {=n-2} joins.

pool.prompt: You join a to l. How high does the join go?
choices: Up to the top of the tall l
Up to the top of small letters
pool.hint: Is l a small letter or a tall letter?
pool.explain: l is a tall letter, so the diagonal join climbs right up to the top of its ascender.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a break letter?
pool.hint: Break letters end with a tail or hook.
pool.explain: y ends with a tail below the line, so it is a break letter. a and w both join.

pool.prompt: You write {n} words. Each has 4 letters and no break letters. How many joins do you make in all?
pool.hint: How many joins does one 4-letter word need?
pool.explain: Each 4-letter word has 3 joins, so {n} words have {=3*n} joins.

pool.prompt: Sam joins w to i by going down to the line, then up. What went wrong?
choices: w ends at the top, so the join should go straight across
pool.hint: Look at where w ends: at the top of the small letters, like o.
pool.explain: w finishes at the top, so it makes a horizontal join across to i. Dipping down makes a loop.

pool.prompt: Which pair uses a diagonal join?
pool.hint: Which first letter ends on the line?
pool.explain: u ends on the line with a flick, so it joins up on a slant to n. o and v end at the top.

pool.prompt: A word has {n} letters. The second letter is g, and no other letter is a break letter. How many joins are there?
pool.hint: We join to g but not from g.
pool.explain: There are {=n-1} gaps. The gap after g stays open, so there are {=n-2} joins.

pool.prompt: In Mia's joined writing, her a is as tall as her h. What should she fix?
choices: Make a small, up to the dashed line
Nothing, letters can be any size
pool.hint: Is a a small letter or a tall letter?
pool.explain: a is a small letter, so it stops at the dashed line. Only tall letters like h reach the top line.

pool.prompt: Is it right to join a to p in the word gap?
choices: Yes, we can join to a break letter
No, never join near a break letter
No, p must be joined from
pool.hint: Break letters are not joined from. Are they joined to?
pool.explain: We do not join from a break letter, but we can join to one. So a joins to p, and the gap after g stays open.
